title: Carriers in Equilibrium
description: How many electrons and holes a semiconductor holds: Fermi–Dirac statistics, intrinsic carriers, doping, the mass-action law and the Fermi level.

study.title: Constants for this subject
study.body:
Unless stated otherwise, silicon at $T$ = 300 K:
- $q = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $k = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K, so $kT$ = 0.0259 eV and $kT/q$ = 0.0259 V
- $E_g$ = 1.12 eV, $n_i = 1.5\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³
- $N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $N_v = 1.04\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³
- $\varepsilon_{Si} = 11.7\,\varepsilon_0$, $\varepsilon_{ox} = 3.9\,\varepsilon_0$ (SiO$_2$), $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-14}$ F/cm
Device physics works in centimetres: concentrations in cm⁻³, mobilities in cm²/V·s, lengths in cm (1 µm = $10^{-4}$ cm).

study.title: Density of states
study.body: How many electron states are there per unit energy? Near the conduction-band edge the density of states grows as the square root of the energy above $E_c$ (and below $E_v$ for holes). A heavier effective mass gives more states. Multiplying by the occupation probability and integrating over the band gives the **effective density of states** $N_c$, as if all states were packed at $E_c$. $N_c$ and $N_v$ grow as $T^{3/2}$.

study.title: Explore: Fermi–Dirac vs Boltzmann
study.body: The probability that a state at energy $E$ is occupied is the **Fermi–Dirac** function. At $E = E_F$ it is exactly ½ at any temperature; the transition from 1 to 0 is a few $kT$ wide. When $E - E_F > 3kT$ the 1 in the denominator hardly matters and $f$ becomes the **Boltzmann** exponential (dashed). Drag $T$: at low temperature the step becomes sharp.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& f(E) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(E - E_F)/kT}}\\ & f(E) \approx e^{-(E - E_F)/kT}\end{aligned}

study.title: Electron and hole concentrations
study.body: Integrating density of states × probability gives the thermal-equilibrium concentrations. The closer $E_F$ lies to $E_c$, the more electrons; the closer to $E_v$, the more holes. These Boltzmann forms hold while $E_F$ stays more than about $3kT$ away from both band edges (a **nondegenerate** semiconductor).
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& n_0 = N_c\, e^{-(E_c - E_F)/kT}\\ & p_0 = N_v\, e^{-(E_F - E_v)/kT}\end{aligned}

study.title: Intrinsic carriers
study.body: In a pure crystal $n_0 = p_0 = n_i$; multiplying $n_0$ and $p_0$ eliminates $E_F$. With the $N_c$ and $N_v$ above the formula gives about $7\times10^9$ cm⁻³ at 300 K, but we use the measured value $1.5\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³. Since $n_i \propto T^{3/2}e^{-E_g/2kT}$ it rises steeply with temperature; scale it from 300 K with the second formula ($E_g$ kept fixed). The intrinsic Fermi level $E_{Fi}$ sits $\tfrac12 kT\ln(N_c/N_v)$ = 0.0128 eV below midgap. On the graph, a sample doped with $N_d = 10^{13}$ cm⁻³ (dashed line) becomes intrinsic above about 415 K.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& n_i^2 = N_cN_v\, e^{-E_g/kT}\\ & n_i(T) = n_i(300)\left(\frac{T}{300}\right)^{3/2} e^{-x}\\ & x = \frac{E_g}{2k}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{300}\right)\end{aligned}

study.title: Doping and the mass-action law
study.body: **Donors** (group V: P, As) have a fifth electron bound by only about 0.045 eV; at 300 K they are fully ionized and give $n_0 \approx N_d$: **n-type**. **Acceptors** (group III: B) grab an electron from a bond, creating a hole: $p_0 \approx N_a$, **p-type**. Whatever the doping, in equilibrium the product $n_0p_0$ stays $n_i^2$, so adding majority carriers suppresses the minority carriers.

study.title: Explore: doping moves the Fermi level
study.body: With both dopants present (**compensation**) only the difference counts. Charge neutrality $n_0 + N_a = p_0 + N_d$ with $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$ gives the formula below (when $N_d > N_a$; swap the roles for $N_a > N_d$). $E_F$ moves above $E_{Fi}$ by $kT\ln(n_0/n_i)$ in n-type material and below it by $kT\ln(p_0/n_i)$ in p-type material. Drag the dopings.

study.title: Worked example
study.body:
Si with $N_d = 10^{16}$ cm⁻³ at 300 K:
- $n_0 \approx N_d$ = $10^{16}$ cm⁻³, since $N_d \gg n_i$
- $p_0 = n_i^2/n_0$ = $2.25\times10^{20}/10^{16}$ = $2.25\times10^{4}$ cm⁻³
- $E_F - E_{Fi} = kT\ln(n_0/n_i)$ = $0.0259\ln(6.67\times10^5)$ = 0.347 eV
- $E_c - E_F = kT\ln(N_c/n_0)$ = $0.0259\ln(2800)$ = 0.206 eV
These two do not add up exactly to $E_c - E_{Fi}$ = 0.573 eV because the measured $n_i$ = 1.5$\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³ is about twice the value $\sqrt{N_cN_v}\,e^{-E_g/2kT} \approx 7\times10^{9}$ cm⁻³ that these $N_c$, $N_v$ and $E_g$ give. Never mix the two in one calculation: use the formula that matches the data you are given.

steps.title: States and their occupation
steps.body: To count carriers we need two things: how many states exist at each energy (the **density of states**, rising as $\sqrt{E - E_c}$ above the conduction-band edge) and the probability that a state is occupied. That probability is the **Fermi–Dirac** function. The **Fermi energy** $E_F$ is where the probability is exactly ½.

steps.prompt: Find the thermal energy $kT$ at $T$ = {{T}} K. ($k = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K)
steps.explanation: $kT$ = 8.617$\times10^{-5}$ eV/K × {{T}} K = **{{8.617e-5*T|eV}}**. Compare 25.9 meV at 300 K. In joules this would be $kT$ = {{1.381e-23*T*1e21||3}}$\times10^{-21}$ J; the eV is much handier next to band energies of about 1 eV.

steps.prompt: A state lies {{dE}} eV **above** the Fermi level at $T$ = {{T}} K. What is the probability that it is occupied by an electron? ($k = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K)
At any temperature, a state exactly at the Fermi energy has a 50 % chance of being occupied.
steps.explanation: At $E = E_F$ the exponent is 0: $f = 1/(1 + e^0) = 1/2$, independent of $T$. That is in fact the definition of $E_F$. Only the **width** of the transition (a few $kT$) changes with temperature.

steps.title: The Boltzmann approximation
steps.body: If $E - E_F$ is more than about $3kT$, then $e^{(E-E_F)/kT} \gg 1$ and the 1 in the denominator can be dropped. The occupation then decays exponentially, like a classical Boltzmann distribution. Conduction-band states in a nondegenerate semiconductor always satisfy this.

steps.prompt: A state lies $E - E_F = {{m}}\,kT$ above the Fermi level. By what percentage does the Boltzmann approximation **overestimate** its occupation probability?
steps.explanation: With $x = (E - E_F)/kT$ = {{m}}: $\frac{f_B}{f} = e^{-x}(1 + e^{x}) = 1 + e^{-x}$. The relative error is $e^{-x} = e^{-{{m}}}$ = **{{100*exp(-m)||3}} %**. At $3kT$ it is about 5 %, which is why $3kT$ is the usual limit.

steps.prompt: At 300 K ($kT$ = 0.0259 eV) a valence-band state lies {{d}} eV **below** $E_F$. What is the probability that it is **empty** (holds a hole)?
steps.explanation: The state is empty with probability $1 - f(E) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(E_F - E)/kT}}$ = $1/(1 + e^{ {{d}}/0.0259 })$ = $1/(1 + e^{ {{d/0.0259||3}} })$ = **{{1/(1+exp(d/0.0259))||3}}**. Holes follow the same statistics mirrored about $E_F$.

steps.prompt: Match each energy with the Fermi–Dirac occupation probability
steps.explanation: $f(E_F) = 1/2$. At $+3kT$: $1/(1 + e^3)$ = 0.047. At $-3kT$: $1/(1 + e^{-3})$ = 0.953 (symmetric: $f(E_F + \Delta) = 1 - f(E_F - \Delta)$). Far above $E_F$ the Boltzmann exponential takes over.

steps.title: Concentrations from the Fermi level
steps.body: Integrating density of states × occupation over the conduction band gives $n_0$; the effective density of states $N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³ (Si, 300 K) collects all states as if they sat at $E_c$. Holes work the same way with $N_v = 1.04\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned}& n_0 = N_c\, e^{-(E_c - E_F)/kT}\\ & p_0 = N_v\, e^{-(E_F - E_v)/kT}\end{aligned}

steps.prompt: In silicon at 300 K the Fermi level lies {{d}} eV below $E_c$. Find the electron concentration $n_0$. ($N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $kT$ = 0.0259 eV)
In silicon at 300 K the Fermi level lies {{d}} eV above $E_v$. Find the hole concentration $p_0$. ($N_v = 1.04\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $kT$ = 0.0259 eV)

steps.title: Intrinsic concentration
steps.body: In a pure crystal $n_0 = p_0 = n_i$. Multiplying $n_0$ and $p_0$ removes $E_F$, so the product depends only on the material and $T$. The steep exponential makes $n_i$ very temperature dependent. At 300 K we use the measured value $n_i = 1.5\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³ for Si.

steps.prompt: Estimate $n_i$ of silicon at {{T}} K by scaling from $1.5\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³ at 300 K: $n_i(T) = n_i(300)\,(T/300)^{3/2}e^{-x}$ with $x = \frac{E_g}{2k}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{300}\right)$, $E_g$ = 1.12 eV fixed and $k = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K.
$N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³ at 300 K. What is $N_c$ of silicon at {{T}} K?
steps.explanation: The effective density of states scales as $T^{3/2}$: $N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}\,({{T}}/300)^{3/2}$ = **{{2.8e19*(T/300)^1.5}} cm⁻³**. The power 3 appears in $n_i^2 \propto T^3$, not in $N_c$.

steps.title: Doping and $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$
steps.body: Phosphorus (group V) has a fifth electron that is bound by only about 0.045 eV, so at room temperature it is free: a **donor**, $n_0 \approx N_d$. Boron (group III) accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, leaving a hole: an **acceptor**, $p_0 \approx N_a$. In equilibrium the product $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$ still holds: extra electrons recombine with holes until the minority concentration drops to $n_i^2/N$.

steps.prompt: Silicon at 300 K is doped with $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ donors (fully ionized). Find the hole concentration $p_0$.
steps.explanation: $n_0 \approx N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ (much larger than $n_i$). Mass action: $p_0 = n_i^2/n_0$ = (1.5$\times10^{10}$)² / {{Nd}} = 2.25$\times10^{20}$ / {{Nd}} = **{{2.25e20/Nd}} cm⁻³**. The minority carriers are suppressed far below $n_i$.

steps.prompt: Adding donors to silicon increases the electron concentration **and** the hole concentration.
steps.explanation: Since $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$ is fixed at a given temperature, raising $n_0$ lowers $p_0$: the extra electrons recombine with holes. Donors make electrons the **majority** and holes a tiny **minority**.

steps.prompt: Silicon at 300 K has $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³. How far is the Fermi level above the intrinsic level, $E_F - E_{Fi}$? ($kT$ = 0.0259 eV)
steps.explanation: $n_0 \approx N_d$, so $E_F - E_{Fi} = kT\ln(n_0/n_i)$ = 0.0259 × ln({{Nd}} / 1.5$\times10^{10}$) = 0.0259 × {{ln(Nd/1.5e10)||3}} = **{{0.0259*ln(Nd/1.5e10)||3}} eV**. Ten times more doping moves $E_F$ up by $kT\ln 10$ = 60 meV.

steps.prompt: Silicon at 300 K has $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³. How far is the Fermi level below the conduction-band edge, $E_c - E_F$? ($N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $kT$ = 0.0259 eV)
steps.explanation: From $n_0 = N_c e^{-(E_c - E_F)/kT}$: $E_c - E_F = kT\ln(N_c/n_0)$ = 0.0259 × ln(2.8$\times10^{19}$ / {{Nd}}) = **{{0.0259*ln(2.8e19/Nd)||3}} eV**. Heavier doping pushes $E_F$ towards $E_c$.

steps.prompt: A silicon sample at 300 K contains $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ donors and $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ acceptors, all ionized.

ask.explanation: Compensation: the acceptors capture {{Na}} of the donor electrons. $n_0 = \frac{N_d - N_a}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{N_d - N_a}{2}\right)^2 + n_i^2}$; since $N_d - N_a \gg n_i$ this is simply $N_d - N_a$ = **{{n0}} cm⁻³**.
$n_0 \approx N_d - N_a$ = {{n0}} cm⁻³, then $p_0 = n_i^2/n_0$ = 2.25$\times10^{20}$ / {{n0}} = **{{2.25e20/n0}} cm⁻³**. Using $N_d$ instead of $N_d - N_a$ is the usual mistake.

steps.prompt: Silicon contains $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ and $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³. Where is the Fermi level?
steps.explanation: Only the net doping counts: $N_d - N_a$ = {{Nd - Na}} cm⁻³. Positive means net donors (n-type, $E_F$ above $E_{Fi}$); negative means net acceptors (p-type, $E_F$ below $E_{Fi}$). The Fermi level is $kT\ln(|N_d - N_a|/n_i)$ = {{0.0259*ln(abs(Nd-Na)/1.5e10)||3}} eV away from $E_{Fi}$.

steps.prompt: Silicon at 300 K. Drag the donor concentration until the Fermi level reaches the dashed target, {{d}} eV above $E_{Fi}$.
steps.explanation: Invert $E_F - E_{Fi} = kT\ln(N_d/n_i)$: $N_d = n_i\,e^{(E_F - E_{Fi})/kT}$ = 1.5$\times10^{10}$ × $e^{ {{d}}/0.0259 }$ = **{{1.5e10*exp(d/0.0259)}} cm⁻³**. Each decade of doping moves $E_F$ by about 60 meV.

steps.prompt: Boron-doped silicon at 300 K has $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³.

ask.prompt: How far is $E_F$ below $E_{Fi}$, i.e. $E_{Fi} - E_F$? ($kT$ = 0.0259 eV)
How far is $E_F$ above the valence-band edge, $E_F - E_v$? ($N_v = 1.04\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $kT$ = 0.0259 eV)

steps.prompt: Match each item with its effect in silicon
steps.explanation: Group-V atoms have one valence electron more than Si, group-III atoms one fewer. When both are present they compensate and only the difference sets the type and the Fermi level.

steps.prompt: A silicon sample with $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ and $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ is p-type.
steps.explanation: Compare the two: $N_a - N_d$ = {{Na - Nd}} cm⁻³. If that is positive there are net acceptors and holes are the majority (p-type); if negative, net donors make it n-type. The majority concentration is about $|N_d - N_a|$ = {{abs(Nd - Na)}} cm⁻³.

steps.prompt: Silicon with $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ is heated to {{T}} K, where $n_i$ = {{ni}} cm⁻³. Find $n_0$ (all donors ionized).
steps.explanation: $n_i$ is no longer negligible, so use the full neutrality result: $n_0 = \frac{N_d}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{N_d}{2}\right)^2 + n_i^2}$ = {{Nd/2}} + √({{(Nd/2)^2}} + {{ni^2}}) = **{{Nd/2 + sqrt((Nd/2)^2 + ni^2)}} cm⁻³**. When $n_i \gg N_d$ the material behaves intrinsically and $n_0 \to n_i$.

steps.prompt: A device doped with $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ stops working once $n_i$ reaches $N_d$. Drag the temperature to that point on the $n_i(T)$ curve of silicon.
steps.explanation: Setting $n_i(T) = N_d$ gives about **{{Tx|K}}** (solve numerically, or read the crossing of the curve with the line). Lighter doping hits the intrinsic limit at lower temperature, and a wider gap pushes it up: this is one reason SiC and GaN devices can run hot.

steps.prompt: $E_{Fi}$ is not exactly at midgap: $E_{Fi} - E_{midgap} = \tfrac12 kT\ln(N_v/N_c)$. How far **below** midgap is $E_{Fi}$ in silicon at {{T}} K? (Both $N_c$ and $N_v$ scale as $T^{3/2}$; at 300 K they are $2.8\times10^{19}$ and $1.04\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³.)
steps.explanation: The ratio $N_c/N_v$ = 2.8/1.04 = 2.69 does not change with $T$. So $E_{midgap} - E_{Fi} = \tfrac12 kT\ln(N_c/N_v)$ = 0.5 × {{8.617e-5*T||3}} eV × ln 2.69 = **{{0.5*8.617e-5*T*ln(2.8/1.04)|eV}}**. Small compared with $E_g/2$ = 0.56 eV: placing $E_{Fi}$ at midgap is usually fine.

steps.prompt: A design rule treats the Boltzmann expressions as valid while $E_c - E_F \ge {{m}}kT$. Up to what donor concentration does that hold in silicon at {{T}} K? ($N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm⁻³ at 300 K, scaling as $T^{3/2}$)
steps.explanation: $N_c({{T}}\ \text{K})$ = 2.8$\times10^{19}$ × ({{T}}/300)$^{3/2}$ = {{2.8e19*(T/300)^1.5}} cm⁻³. Setting $E_c - E_F = {{m}}kT$ in $n_0 = N_c e^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT}$: $N_d = N_c e^{-{{m}}}$ = **{{2.8e19*(T/300)^1.5*exp(-m)}} cm⁻³** (assuming full ionization). Heavier doping pushes $E_F$ closer to $E_c$: towards a **degenerate** semiconductor, where Fermi–Dirac integrals are needed. The usual limit is $3kT$ (Boltzmann error about 5 %); at $2kT$ the error is already about 14 %.

steps.prompt: A silicon wafer is known to contain $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ donors plus an unknown acceptor concentration. At 300 K its Fermi level is {{dEF||4}} eV above $E_{Fi}$. Find $N_a$. ($kT$ = 0.0259 eV)
An n-type silicon sample with $N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³ is cooled from 300 K to 20 K. What happens to $n_0$?
options: It drops far below $N_d$: the donor electrons freeze out onto their donor atoms
It stays at $N_d$: donors are always ionized
steps.explanation: The donor level is about 0.045 eV below $E_c$, which is many $kT$ at 20 K ($kT$ = 1.7 meV). The electrons fall back into the donor states (**freeze-out**), so $n_0 \ll N_d$ = {{Nd}} cm⁻³. Between roughly 100 K and 450 K (for moderate doping) $n_0 \approx N_d$: the **extrinsic** range where devices operate.

steps.prompt: Order the temperature ranges of a doped semiconductor from **cold to hot**
steps.explanation: At low $T$ there is not enough thermal energy to ionize the donors. Over a wide middle range every donor has given its electron and $n_0 = N_d$, independent of $T$. At high $T$ thermal generation across the gap takes over and the doping no longer matters.

steps.prompt: Boron-doped silicon with $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ operates at {{T}} K, where $n_i$ = {{ni}} cm⁻³. Find $E_{Fi} - E_F$. ($k = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K)
steps.explanation: $kT$ = {{kT||3}} eV and $p_0 \approx N_a$ (still $\gg n_i$). $E_{Fi} - E_F = kT\ln(p_0/n_i)$ = {{kT||3}} × ln({{Na}} / {{ni}}) = **{{kT*ln(Na/ni)||3}} eV**. At 300 K it would be {{0.0259*ln(Na/1.5e10)||3}} eV: as $T$ rises, $n_i$ grows and $E_F$ moves back towards $E_{Fi}$.
